1:
Four notes open by objecting to the chapter division. Gill calls it strange that the dividers should separate this verse from the one before, since it belongs manifestly to the foregoing discourse and has no connection with what follows. Henry says the same. Clarke says the chapter should have begun at the exhortation to prayer. Ellicott’s note here is nothing but the outline of the household code, which ends its third division at this verse and so makes the point without arguing it.

Robertson observes that the apostle shifts from an adjective to an abstract noun for the second term, a word he uses only here and in one other place, and remarks that if employers always did this there would be no labour problem. Calvin reads the same word as distributive rather than arithmetical, a right proportioned to the circumstances, station or calling of individuals. Wesley makes the pair a contract and a surplus: just according to your agreement, equitable even beyond its letter. Henry unfolds it — be faithful to promises, do not keep back the hire of the labourers, require no more than servants can perform, supply proper food and physic — and this though they be of another country and a different religion.

Barnes turns the verse into an argument about the institution behind it. The persons meant are probably bondmen, who could not enforce a just claim by appealing to the laws; and the apostles, he holds, designed no violent disruption of these bonds, but did mean to represent the condition as hard and undesirable, to instruct slaves to take the earliest opportunity of freedom, and to lay down principles that would lead masters to emancipate and the thing at last to be abolished. Clarke concedes the same premise in a sentence and finds the exhortation the more proper for it.

The reason at the end checks presumption. Calvin says masters, looking down as from aloft, despise the condition of servants and think themselves bound by no law, so the apostle beats down their presumption, both parties being equally subject to God. Henry turns it into a rule of measure, that a master should deal with his servants as he expects God to deal with him. Robertson calls it a wholesome reminder that the eye above is on the conduct of masters towards those they employ.

On continuing in prayer the word is divided carefully. Gill denies that continuance means always formally praying, or that saints are always in praying frames; it intends frequency and constancy, set against both entire omission and performance now and then. Barnes triples the watching: watch for favourable opportunities, watch that the mind may be in a right frame when you pray, and watch that when it is you do not neglect to pray. Robertson adds that the verb means to hold strongly to a thing and the participle for watching is a late form on a perfect stem. Calvin admits that no exact order is to be looked for here, since otherwise the apostle would have begun with prayer; he finds assiduity and alacrity commended, the second against coldness, and explains the thanksgiving as a guard, since God must be asked for present necessities in such a way that past favours are not forgotten, and we must not murmur when he does not gratify us at once. Henry connects the verse back to the master, making it his duty to pray daily with his household and be concerned for their souls as well as their bodies. Clarke generalises furthest: no station can be filled without the grace peculiar to it, and he asks how few wives or husbands ever pray for the grace suited to their place — which he calls the origin of family broils in general.
3:
The request for prayer is taken first as humility. Gill says it is made not in dissimulation but in true lowliness, the apostle being sensible of his own weakness and of how much the prayers of even the meanest in the church might do for him. Calvin draws the consequence: who now would dare to despise the intercessions of brethren, which the apostle declares himself to need? He then calls it worse than childish to argue from a man commending himself to the prayers of the living that the departed are to be implored for us.

The door is the phrase everyone stops on, and one note dissents on what it opens. Clarke traces the metaphor through three other places where the word means an opportunity for a work, as the best Latin writers also use it. Robertson gives the same parallels and finds it comforting that the greatest of all preachers should ask prayer to be set free to preach, being at bottom a prisoner because of his preaching to the Gentiles. Ellicott separates the cases: elsewhere the opened door is external opportunity, here the removal of all internal impediments to preaching. Wesley reads it the same inward way, as utterance given so the mouth may be opened boldly. Barnes keeps it simple, that the apostle desired liberty to preach and asked them to pray it be restored. Calvin says the next clause states the difficulty more strongly, since what is desired is an undaunted confidence such as befits the majesty of the gospel; and he makes a rule of it, that we are not to give way to the fury of adversaries but to strive even to death, and, this being beyond our power, to pray that we be not left destitute of confidence. Robertson notices a smaller thing: wonderful as this preaching was, the preacher was never satisfied with it, and what preacher can be? Gill takes the manifesting ministerially, God alone making the mystery manifest in a saving way.

The turn to outsiders draws the fullest comment. Calvin gives three reasons why regard is to be had to those without: lest we put a stumbling-block before the blind, since nothing happens more readily than that unbelievers are driven from bad to worse by our imprudence until they hold religion in abhorrence; lest occasion be given for detracting from the honour of the gospel and persecutions be stirred up; and lest, mingling with them at meals, we be defiled and little by little become profane. Chrysostom grounds it in the charge to be wise as serpents and harmless as doves, and marks the limitation: against our own members we need no such caution, since it is not the same to be among enemies as among friends. He guards it from being a counsel of craft, since craft is not wisdom but senselessness — give them no handle where they do you no harm, and let the preaching alone be the ground of war. Barnes turns it into an argument about reputation: men of the world judge religion not from its profession or its books but from the daily walk of church members, and know well enough when they are inconsistent. Henry adds the double caution: take no hurt from those without, and give none. Clarke uses the word without for an excursus on the pale of the Church, explaining the term from the stake that makes an enclosure, granting the maxim that there is no salvation outside it, and denying the use made of it by any one body that arrogates the title to itself alone. Ellicott compares the parallel epistle, where the same wisdom guards against recklessness within while here it watches dangers outside; and Robertson gives the redeeming of the time its plainest sense, that we all have the same time and the apostle buys it up in the open market by using it rightly.
6:
The salt divides them, and the division is real. Barnes reports that salt among the Greeks was the emblem of wit, and rejects a gloss making the clause mean only courteous and agreeable rather than morose — true so far as it goes, but not all that is meant. Clarke takes the preserving sense, quotes a rabbinic saying that prayer with a word omitted is like boiled pottage without salt, and warns that a harsh way of defending Christian doctrine serves only to repel men. Robertson makes it wit outright, notes that our word for the indecent is this word degenerated into vulgarity, and says grace and salt make an ideal combination — adding, of the charge to know how to answer each man, the question who does know. Ellicott hears the Lord’s own saying about salt behind it, then argues away from the preserving sense: the context makes the use of the salt the answering of every man, so the seasoning is probably against insipidity, the speech being primarily kindled by grace and secondarily given point, effective for the inquirer or against the scoffer. Calvin refuses the whole line. He grants that classical writers use the term for witticisms, but says the apostle does not speak of these; indeed, since witticisms are insinuating and generally procure favour, he indirectly forbids believers the familiar use of them, reckoning as tasteless everything that does not edify. Gill hesitates between subject and manner: the speech is either about grace, so that saints confer on the work of grace upon their souls, or in the exercise of grace, in truth and sincerity without flattery. Wesley gives the shortest gloss of all, seasoned with the grace of God as flesh is with salt.

The messenger is treated as a pledge. Calvin makes the sending the argument: though in prison and in danger of his life the apostle consults their interests, so that the body is under confinement while the mind roams far and wide; and he finds prudence in the choice, a fit person sent to withstand the false apostles, while Epaphras is kept back so that they may hear from the one what they had learned from the other and see how great an agreement there is among true teachers. Henry explains why nothing is written: the bearer would tell it more fully by word of mouth, and the churches cannot but desire to know a good minister’s state — noting that an apostle owns a faithful minister for a brother, and that it adds much to the beauty of the ministry when ministers support one another’s reputation. Clarke gives the practical reason, that the messenger could supply the detail in full and that some of it would not have been prudent to commit to writing. Robertson compares the parallel epistle and finds the same verb and epithets, with fellow-servant added here, which one commentator explains by the apostle having already used that word of Epaphras. Gill supplies the biography: an Asian, whose name means fortunate and answers to a Latin name in another epistle, said to have been one of the seventy and afterwards bishop of Chalcedon.

At the next verse two notes prefer a variant. Clarke reports that many manuscripts read that ye may know our affairs rather than that he may know yours, and thinks it the true reading, since the man was sent not to learn their affairs but to make the apostle’s state known and comfort them. Robertson agrees that this is the correct text against the third-person singular, and adds that the last verb should be rendered comfort here rather than exhort. Tertullian’s note here is not on this epistle at all: it observes that the brevity of the letter to Philemon alone protected it from Marcion, and wonders that he received that letter while rejecting three that treat of ecclesiastical discipline.
9:
Whether the second messenger is the runaway of the other epistle is settled by everyone but one. Gill, Barnes, Clarke, Ellicott and Robertson all identify him, Robertson calling him co-bearer of the letter and praised on a par with the first, runaway slave though he is. Calvin alone doubts it: it can scarcely be believed that this is the slave of Philemon, since the name of a thief and a fugitive would have been liable to reproach. The editorial matter printed with him answers the doubt from a later writer, who made the phrase one of you an undesigned coincidence placing Philemon at Colosse.

Barnes uses the same phrase differently. He doubts the man was of the rank the modern word slave denotes, since the apostle would not have told a community of masters that a runaway was one of themselves — and asks whether a minister in the Northern States, sending a letter by a fugitive to masters in the South, would say so. Clarke stays with the local fact, that a countryman lately converted could give the news more acceptably, and adds that the transactions at Rome might not have been prudent to write down. Ellicott sees in the two epithets a commentary on the rules for slaves and masters just given.

The salutations raise a difficulty nobody solves. Aristarchus is a fellow-prisoner here, while in the letter sent at the same time that title falls to Epaphras and he is merely a fellow-labourer. Clarke states it flatly: one of them is wrong, though it is uncertain which, unless both were prisoners — and suggests they may have been imprisoned about the same time but not together. Ellicott finds the variation a mark of genuineness in the epistles and admits it can be accounted for only by conjecture, such as their alternately sharing the captivity. Robertson reports that one commentator argues for a literal imprisonment shared by turns. Wesley says Epaphras was such for a time. Calvin infers that others were imprisoned with the apostle at Rome, and guesses that his enemies at first deterred the pious from helping him by threats.

On Mark the notes turn to the old quarrel, which Barnes recalls separated two apostles who afterwards became reconciled. Henry draws the moral, that a man who had differed with him over this Mark not only was reconciled but commended him to the churches — if men have been guilty of a fault it must not always be remembered against them, and we must forget as well as forgive. Robertson puts it shortest, once rejected for his defection but now cordially commended because he had made good again, and settles the disputed word of kinship as cousin rather than nephew. Wesley explains the odd tense of the directions by ancient usage, the ancients adapting their language to the time of reading a letter and not, as we do, to the time of writing.

The last name provokes two independent attacks on the same target. Clarke observes that only three of the circumcision were then helping the apostle, and reasons that the chief of the apostles cannot have been at Rome or he would have been named — so the keystone of the papal arch is pulled out. Calvin asks the same in his own words: either the man has been shamefully passed over here, and not without injustice, or else those speak falsely who maintain he was then at Rome. Ellicott takes the juxtaposition to show that the brethren who held aloof in envy were themselves of the circumcision. Gill and Robertson both note that the Hebrew name is the common one and the surname its Latin equivalent, Robertson adding that our word for a soothing medicine descends from the word for their comfort. Wesley ends with a question: what then can we expect, that all our fellow-workers should be a comfort to us?
12:
Chrysostom alone asks why the commendation is there. To praise a man is a sign of love, and to pray for him breeds love in return; the apostle commends this one to open a door for his teaching, since reverence towards a teacher is the disciples’ own advantage. He weighs the verb too: it says not simply praying but striving, trembling and fearing. Barnes and Clarke both render it agonizing, Barnes adding that it affirms nothing about anyone having been absolutely perfect. Calvin makes it a portrait of a good pastor whom distance cannot induce to forget his church, and turns it on the hearers, who are to count on real assistance from their pastor’s prayers.

Two notes prefer a variant in the same clause. Clarke reports that almost all manuscripts of the best recension read fully persuaded for complete, and explains it as a persuasion leaving the mind neither room nor inclination to doubt. Ellicott agrees, and reads the two epithets as aimed at the Gnostic teachers’ claim to an exclusive perfection in wisdom, the true fellow-worker praying that this perfection may belong to all and rest not on secret knowledge but on the revealed will of God. Robertson notes the same participle. Wesley gives the plainest gloss, no longer babes but grown to the measure of the stature of Christ.

The three cities draw out the antiquarian. Barnes describes Hierapolis, the hot springs it was celebrated for and the temples it was named from, adding that the Turks now call it the Cotton-Tower from the white cliffs about it, and that it is forsaken though its ruins show it was once among the most splendid cities of the East. Clarke names the gods worshipped there from coins still extant, and prefers a reading of much labour to much zeal. Robertson calls it the third of the three cities in the valley that never saw the apostle’s face, all three evangelised by the same man and in peril from the same teachers. Ellicott finds in one man’s responsibility for three churches, as in the charges to Timothy and Titus, the link between the apostolate of that period and the episcopacy of the future. Gill says only that the apostle was an eye and ear witness of the man’s fervency.

The physician is identified by everyone except Calvin. Gill, Barnes, Robertson and Ellicott all take him for the evangelist; Clarke reports the doubt of those who make them different, since elsewhere the evangelist has his simple name, and explains the Greek word as covering surgeon and physician and dispenser of medicines alike. Calvin dissents outright: the evangelist was too well known to need such a designation and would have had a more magnificent title, fellow-helper or companion in his conflicts; so he conjectures the evangelist was absent and this is another man of the same name. Gill adds a legend, that Luke had been a scholar of Galen, or his sister’s son, and set out with him for Judea to test the report of the miracles, Galen dying on the road while Luke came to Christ. Barnes prefers soberer evidence, that the writer was probably a proselyte, and that there are incidental signs in his two books of a man who observed events with the eye of one who practised the healing art. Ellicott notices the emphasis of the Greek, the physician, the beloved one, against a bare name for the next man, and passes on to the last notice of the two together. Robertson says the same warmly, that the affection was not one-sided and it is beautiful to see preacher and physician warm friends, adding that two evangelists were with the apostle at that moment, possibly with copies of their Gospels beside them. Wesley leaves a doubt hanging in five words, that such he had been at least, if he was not then.
15:
The first salutation hangs on a pronoun nobody can settle. Ellicott reports three readings — the church in his house, in her house, and, as he thinks best, in their house — the second requiring a feminine name-form the Greek hardly bears. Robertson concludes flatly that it is not possible to tell whether the house was hers or his; he adds that separate buildings were not used for worship until the third century, and Clarke that there were then no consecrated places, the setting apart of a room being held sufficient. Calvin takes the case as a rule: in one household a pattern is laid down for all, that they be so many little churches. Barnes and Wesley say only that nothing further is known of the man.

The letter to be exchanged has produced a crowd of conjectures, and four are here. Clarke lays out three: that it was written from Laodicea to the apostle, which he calls forced and far-fetched; that it is the epistle we call to the Ephesians; or that a distinct letter is lost, one under that name being known to Jerome, who calls it apocryphal. Calvin holds the first, denying that the other letter was written by the apostle and doubly that it was written to Laodicea, and denouncing the forgery circulating under that title as a gross imposture and an insipid thing. Wesley agrees in five words, that the letter is from Laodicea and not to it. Robertson holds the second, that the circular we call Ephesians went to Laodicea and was passed on. Ellicott declines to choose but draws something larger from the direction: here is the method by which the apostolic letters were first published, and in the order to exchange them the way they came to be received as authoritative — canonised, that is; and the likelihood of such public reading bears on the authenticity of books later reckoned doubtful. Barnes gives the city its history. Calvin generalises: the letters were addressed first to particular churches, but since they contain doctrine always in force it is of no importance what title they bear, for the subject matter belongs to us.

Whether the word to Archippus is a rebuke divides them. Gill assumes it, the man being negligent and therefore to be spoken to. Calvin half assumes it, and draws from the indirect address a principle: the charge is given to the church so that they may know they must themselves remonstrate if they see their pastor cold, and that the pastor must not refuse to be admonished — ministers of the word having signal authority, but not an authority exempt from laws. Barnes denies the premise, finding no evidence that remissness was implied. Clarke denies it by a date: if this is the man called fellow-soldier in the letter written the same year, he cannot have been at Rome and a delinquent at Colosse at once. Ellicott leaves censure alone but finds it strange to send through one church a message to a chief pastor of another. Wesley turns it on the hearers, that it is the flock’s duty to try those who claim to be sent, and defines the office against its abuse: not a lordship but a service, an obligation to be the servant of all. Robertson keeps to the verb: fulfilling the ministry means going on filling it full, a lifetime job.

The autograph is a guarantee. Gill says it was added to prevent counterfeits; Clarke calls it the means by which every epistle was authenticated; Ellicott notes that the invariable autograph salutation has become the universal Christian blessing. On the last three words Barnes says they were to remember he suffered on their account, Clarke that such a man being in bonds was itself the fullest proof of the gospel’s truth, and Robertson that the chain clanked afresh as the pen was taken up.
